overview: Sigma's DeathClip shifts the player's local position at the exact moment of death and then runs a chat command. On the pre-update where getHealth() first reads 0, the VClip mode teleports the player straight up by the DIST setting, default 2, while the HClip mode shifts horizontally by twice the DIST along the yaw plus 90 degrees and nudges y by 0.001; four ticks later the module sends the MESSAGE command, default /sethome. The position change is a local setPosition that reaches the server only through the movement packets the client continues to emit while the death screen is up.

sections.p: The module registers three settings: the CLIP mode option with VClip default and HClip, the DIST distance with default 2.0 and range -10 to 10, and the MESSAGE string defaulting to /sethome. The pre-update handler checks getHealth() == 0 and the dead flag: the first such tick picks the mode, writes the new position with setPosition, increments waitTicks and sets dead; the flag clears again only once health rises above 0. While dead, waitTicks increments each pre-update and at 4 the module calls ChatUtil.sendChat with the configured message, then resets the counter.

setPosition is a local teleport that sends nothing by itself. What carries the shift is the C03 stream: the fork's NetHandlerPlayServer.processPlayer has no isDead early-out, only the end-crystal conquest guard, and the client keeps ticking the player entity while the death screen is open, so the next position packet after the clip already contains the shifted coordinates. Vanilla's moved-too-quickly gate squares min(delta, motion) per axis and motion is near zero at death, so a 2-block vertical or 4-block horizontal shift passes it. The module's own guaranteed send is the C01 chat message four ticks later, built by ChatUtil.sendChat through the vanilla sendChatMessage path, and that is the only packet it constructs directly.

The clip only matters if the server command executes against the player's reported position: Bukkit's getLocation returns the server entity position, which follows the accepted C03 stream, so a /sethome sent after the clip records the shifted spot. On servers whose commands use their own anchor, fixed spawns or bed points, the shift is inert. The cheat therefore sits on the server's willingness to trust the dying player's last reported position, and the wire artifact is one ordinary command among the death screen's traffic.

files.label: DeathClip.java (death-time position shift)
files.explanation: The whole module. The pre-update handler fires the clip once per death: VClip writes setPosition(posX, posY + distance, posZ), HClip shifts by distance times 2 along the yaw plus 90 degrees with a 0.001 y nudge so the position change is guaranteed to differ. waitTicks then counts up to 4 pre-updates while dead and fires ChatUtil.sendChat with the MESSAGE string, default /sethome. The dead flag resets when health rises above 0, so a fresh death re-arms the clip; the module sends no movement packet itself, relying on the client's own C03 stream to carry the shifted position.

files.label: ChatUtil.java (command send path)
files.explanation: sendChat routes through mc.thePlayer.sendChatMessage, the vanilla chat path that forwards a slash-prefixed message as C01PacketChatMessage unless it matches a client-side command. /sethome is not a client command, so the four-tick-delayed message reaches the server as a plain C01. sendChat_NoFilter shows the alternative direct-queue construction the module does not use; the module picks the vanilla path, which means the command is subject to the same chat handling and rate limits as any player message.

countering.label: SurvivalFly (movement physics envelope)
countering.explanation: SurvivalFly validates each move against a physics envelope computed from the block cache and the previous move's momentum, with set-backs on violation. If the server processes the dying player's movement, the clipped position arrives as a one-tick vertical or horizontal jump: a 2-block instant ascent exceeds the jump-scale vertical allowance and a 4-block horizontal shift exceeds the horizontal envelope, so the check flags the first post-clip C03. The Sigma fork's own processPlayer has no dead guard, which is exactly the surface the module relies on, and where that move is accepted the envelope is the direct counter.

countering.label: Flight (vertical-clip scan)
countering.explanation: Arc v2's Flight runs its vertical-clip branch whenever a vertical move exceeds 0.99 blocks while the player is not climbing, on a step, in liquid or under velocity: it scans every solid block between the safe location and the destination and flags the move if any is solid. The VClip's 2-block ascent crosses whatever ceiling sits above the death spot, so the branch fires exactly when the clip passes through solid geometry; in open air the ascension ledger, vertical speed over the jump cap, still scores the move.

countering.label: chat Commands (command rate ledger)
countering.explanation: NCP's chat Commands scores slash-commands on a frequency ledger, with default thresholds of commandsLevel 10 and a short-term count of 3 per 18 ticks over an ActionFrequency window, cancelling command loops that exceed them. A single /sethome per death is one command separated by seconds, far below the ledger's limits, so the check passes; it is the honest boundary on the module's one guaranteed send and would only engage if a scripted death loop spammed the command repeatedly.

countering.label: chat Text (content and frequency scoring)
countering.explanation: NCP's chat Text scores each message through letter-shape analysis, per-word notLetter ratios against a 0.5 optimum, and a per-player frequency model, flagging template or repetitive traffic. One configured command per death reads as ordinary chat, so the check stays quiet; like Commands it bounds the module's actual wire artifact rather than the clip itself. The entry is the second honest boundary on the C01 side, since no movement check can score a position shift on servers that drop dead-player moves entirely.
